Share of the Erdős problems listed in the erdosproblems database (github.com/teorth/erdosproblems, data/statistics_history.csv; the problems of erdosproblems.com) whose status is solved (proved, disproved or otherwise solved: column total_solved) out of all problems listed (total_problems), at the last database snapshot by the end of the obs month (UTC); the list itself grows

Q-Day qubit gap: how many times more qubits breaking RSA-2048 needs than the largest good-enough quantum computer has; qday-rsa2048-qubits-needed (fewest physical qubits in the best published estimate, at 0.1% error) divided by qday-largest-device-qubits (physical qubits of the largest device with two-qubit error <= 0.1%); 1 = enough qubits exist. Derived by the collector at each date either input changes (obs = that date), 3 significant digits. Fine print: it counts qubits only; the device's speed (ion traps run 100-1000x slower than the 1 us cycle the estimates assume), connectivity (some estimates need long-range links) and error rates other than the two-qubit gate are not checked, error rates better than 0.1% earn no credit, and device figures are as reported by their builders. What 1x means in time: factoring then takes about the best estimate's own runtime on hardware as fast as it assumes; for the Pinnacle estimate (arXiv 2602.11457 v2, May 2026, Table VI, at 0.1% error) about a month with 94k qubits at a 1 us code cycle, and more qubits buy speed (135k: a week; 381k: a day). Slower hardware needs more qubits for the same time: at a 10 us cycle 94k qubits take a year (a month needs 193k), at 100 us a month needs 1.0M, and trapped ions (about 1 ms) need 871k qubits for a year or 9.5M for a month, i.e. roughly 10-100x the gap's target

Neurons whose synapse-level wiring was reconstructed and proofread in the largest published connectome of one animal (a whole brain or nervous system, or a partial volume), by the publication's own neuron count (non-neuronal cells and neurons without reconstructed connectivity excluded); obs = the publication date (paper or dataset release)

Highest superconducting critical temperature at ambient pressure (Tc as the publication reports it, typically the resistive or magnetic onset) among materials whose superconductivity (zero resistance and Meissner effect) has been reported by at least two independent groups; metastable phases retained at ambient pressure count; obs = the date the record was established (the confirming report, not the first claim). Room temperature is about 293 K

HPL Rmax of the rank-1 system on the TOP500 list (top500.org, published each June and November), in PFlop/s; obs = the list month (YYYY-06 or YYYY-11). Only systems submitted to the list count (large private AI clusters are often absent)
Confirmed exoplanets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive (Planetary Systems Composite table, pscomppars) with discovery year <= obs year, counted in the archive at retrieval; obs = calendar year

Fewest physical qubits sufficient to factor a 2048-bit RSA modulus according to the best published resource estimate (a paper or preprint with a full resource count, every quantum resource counted as qubits, e.g. no separate quantum memory, and a runtime of at most a year) at a physical error rate of about 0.1% (10^-3) per operation, on any hardware architecture; value = its stated qubit count ('less than N' records N); obs = the estimate's publication date. Input of qday-qubit-gap

Physical qubits in the largest gate-based quantum computer whose two-qubit gate error averaged over the whole device is at most 0.1% (fidelity >= 99.9%) and that supports mid-circuit measurement with real-time feedback (needed for error correction), as reported by its builder for one full system (not a subset, a test chip or unlinked modules); obs = the date that device's figures were first published. The error bar is the assumption of the qday-rsa2048-qubits-needed estimates. Input of qday-qubit-gap
